questions.subtopic: 2A1 Engagement objectives and scope. A requested engagement outside the plan
questions.question: After a ransomware attack, a Uruguayan port operator's board asks internal auditor Facundo for assurance on the controls the attackers bypassed, work outside the approved plan. How does the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement apply MOST accurately?

options.A: It applies, with each requirement assessed and any exclusion justified
options.B: It is recommended, as the work falls outside the approved plan
options.C: It applies after the plan is amended, then each requirement is assessed
options.D: It applies to the controls the board names, with others excluded

questions.key_concept: A requested assurance engagement on a Topical Requirement's topic must conform; the requester's focus shapes objectives, but each requirement is assessed and exclusions justified.
questions.pre_read: Ask which trigger applies, whether the work is assurance, and who decides which requirements are excluded and why.
questions.correct_explanation: A request for work outside the plan is one of the three triggers, and the work is assurance, so conformance is mandatory. The board's focus on the bypassed controls shapes the objectives, but Facundo still assesses every requirement for applicability and documents the reason for each exclusion. Option D lets the requester's wording stand in for that reason, though Standard 13.3's considerations ask whether a request to include or exclude items limits the scope.

wrong_explanations.B: Recommended conformance is the rule for advisory work. This request is for assurance, and a request outside the plan is itself one of the triggers.
wrong_explanations.C: The request itself is a trigger, so applicability does not wait for a plan change. Changing the plan is a separate matter for the chief audit executive and the board.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the board's request shapes the objectives, but each requirement is still assessed, and an exclusion needs Facundo's documented rationale, not the requester's wording.

tips: Eliminate: B, because recommended conformance is the advisory rule and this is assurance, and C, because a request outside the plan is itself a trigger.
Final two: A beats D because the requester shapes the objectives, but the internal auditor assesses each requirement and documents every exclusion's reason.
Exam cue: on CIA questions where a stakeholder narrows a requested engagement, the internal auditor usually still assesses every requirement and records why any is excluded.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Engagement objectives and scope. An input the Standards require
questions.question: Internal auditor Ingrid has three days to plan assurance on a Swedish ferry line's ticket refunds. Which input do the Standards MOST clearly require Ingrid to gather?

options.A: Workpapers from the last refund engagement, where one was done
options.B: Other assurance providers' recent results on refunds, where any exist
options.C: The company's risk tolerance for refunds, where one is set
options.D: Refund staff's views from a short survey, where time allows

questions.key_concept: Standard 13.2 requires gathering the organization's risk tolerance, if set; earlier workpapers, other providers' results and staff surveys are optional sources.
questions.pre_read: Sort the options into what Standard 13.2 requires and what its considerations offer as ways to gather information.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2's requirements list what internal auditors must gather to understand an activity, and the organization's risk tolerance, where one is set, is on that list beside the strategy, the plan's risk assessment and the activity's processes. Option B is a source the considerations suggest, beside earlier workpapers and surveys: useful, but not required.

wrong_explanations.A: If an earlier engagement identified the risks, Standard 13.2 asks only that its risk assessment be reviewed and updated; old workpapers are an optional source in the considerations.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: other providers' results are a useful input to objectives, but Standard 13.2 lists them among optional ways to gather information, not among the required items.
wrong_explanations.D: Surveys are one way to gather information under the considerations. Time pressure aside, the Standards do not require a staff survey in planning.

tips: Eliminate: A, because earlier workpapers are an optional source, and D, because a staff survey is one way to gather information, not a required input.
Final two: C beats B because Standard 13.2 requires the risk tolerance, where set, while other providers' results are an optional source.
Exam cue: on CIA questions asking what the Standards require, pick the item the requirement names over sound sources the considerations list.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Engagement objectives and scope. Testing a newly added objective
questions.question: During a Kenyan tea estate's payroll engagement, the chief audit executive approves internal auditor Wairimu's new objective on pickers' pay, and the payroll manager is told. What must Wairimu MOST clearly do before testing it?

options.A: Have the board approve the new objective, as scope has grown
options.B: Add criteria and tasks for it to the work program, for approval
options.C: Agree with the payroll manager which criteria the objective uses
options.D: Record the change so the final communication can explain it

questions.key_concept: A new objective needs its own criteria and tasks in the work program, approved before testing; approving the objective alone is not enough.
questions.pre_read: Two approvals are involved: the objective's and the work program's. Ask which is still missing, and which options are musts.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.6 requires the work program to name criteria for each objective, the tasks and the internal auditor assigned, and to be approved before it is carried out and promptly after any change. Approving the objective under Standard 13.3 does not approve the work program. Option C is good practice from Standard 13.4's considerations, informing management of the criteria and documenting those agreed, but it is a should, not the requirement.

wrong_explanations.A: The chief audit executive approves objectives and any change to them; the board approves the internal audit plan, not one engagement's objectives.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: telling the payroll manager the criteria, and documenting those agreed, is a should from Standard 13.4's considerations; the approved work program is the must.
wrong_explanations.D: Management has already been told of the change. A note kept for the final communication does not replace a revised, approved work program before testing.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the chief audit executive, not the board, approves an engagement's objectives, and D, because a note for the final communication is not the missing step.
Final two: B beats C because approving the objective did not approve the work program; the revised program, with the objective's criteria, is a must, while agreeing criteria is a should.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about a change midway, check each step in turn: approve the objectives and scope, approve the revised work program, tell management.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Choosing evaluation criteria. A criterion with no threshold
questions.question: Internal auditor Mere, planning a Fijian water utility's payments engagement, reads that urgent payments may be approved afterward, with no limit on how many or how late. Which step BEST settles the criterion?

options.A: Adopt the late-approval rate peer utilities report as normal
options.B: Size the sample large enough to find late-approved payments
options.C: Confirm that the approval rule sits in a board-approved policy
options.D: Ask whether the utility set an acceptable level of late approvals

questions.key_concept: A criterion needs a yardstick for comparison; check whether the organization has set a satisfactory level of control before measuring results against it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the policy leaves open, and whose yardstick should close it before results are compared.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.4's considerations ask internal auditors to find out whether the organization has set a satisfactory level of control. A policy that allows late approvals with no limit cannot show how many is too many until that level is known. Option A borrows an outside norm: comparison informs judgment, but the utility's own level comes first, and without one criteria are worked out with senior management or the board.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: comparing with other organizations' criteria is sound research, but a peer norm informs judgment; it does not replace the level the utility itself sets or agrees.
wrong_explanations.B: Sample size belongs to the work program and depends on the criterion. Until an acceptable level is known, no sample can say whether late approvals are too many.
wrong_explanations.C: Criteria need not be written in a board-approved policy; procedures and targets can serve. The gap here is the missing limit on late approvals, not where the rule sits.

tips: Eliminate: B, because sampling is designed after the criterion is usable, and C, because criteria need not sit in a board-approved policy to be adequate.
Final two: D beats A because the organization's own satisfactory level of control comes first; a peer rate informs the judgment but does not set it.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about vague criteria, look for the option that finds the organization's own threshold before borrowing one from outside.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Planning around key risks and controls. A strategic measure that is on target
questions.question: Planning assurance on a Ghanaian microlender's growth strategy for small-business loans, internal auditor Kofi sees loan volume, its sole measure, is on target. Which planning conclusion is BEST?

options.A: Lending risks look managed, since the strategic measure is on target
options.B: Volume figures need testing before lending risks are rated
options.C: Credit quality risk needs rating, as no current measure tracks it
options.D: Management needs to add a credit quality measure before risks are rated

questions.key_concept: A measure on target shows one result, not that risks are managed; planning identifies the significant risks the measures leave unwatched.
questions.pre_read: Trace the chain from the strategy to its risks to the measures, and ask which risk no measure would reveal.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 requires Kofi to understand the strategy and objectives, identify the potentially significant risks to them and identify the measures management uses. Volume alone cannot show whether loans go to borrowers who cannot repay, so credit quality is a risk to rate. Option B delays the risk assessment: the reliability of volume data matters for later tests, but it does not decide which risks to rate.

wrong_explanations.A: An on-target measure shows a result, not that risks are managed. Volume can rise while credit checks weaken, so the risks still need assessing.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the reliability of the volume data matters when it is used as evidence, but planning still rates the risks, including those no measure tracks.
wrong_explanations.D: Adding a measure may become a recommendation once the risk is assessed, but management chooses its measures, and planning rates the risk now instead of waiting.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a measure on target does not show risks are managed, and D, because management chooses its measures and planning does not wait for a new one.
Final two: C beats B because planning rates the significant risks now; testing the volume figures is later work that does not decide which risks matter.
Exam cue: on CIA planning questions, follow strategy to risks to measures, and look for the significant risk that the current measures would not reveal.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Planning around key risks and controls. A framework-based cyber work program
questions.question: Internal auditor Ivana will plan a Croatian credit union's cybersecurity assurance engagement from the function's existing work program, which is built on the NIST framework. What should Ivana do FIRST with that program?

options.A: Use it as the scope, since NIST goes deeper than the requirement
options.B: Replace it with a program built from the Topical Requirement
options.C: Keep its tests and add the requirement's steps alongside them
options.D: Map its planned tests to each requirement to confirm coverage

questions.key_concept: An IT control framework helps coverage but does not prove it: reconcile framework-based tests to the Topical Requirement and document the mapping.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a framework gives an engagement, and what the Topical Requirement still demands of the internal auditor.
questions.correct_explanation: The Cybersecurity Topical Requirement's user guide asks internal auditors to reconcile tests built on frameworks such as NIST or COBIT to the requirement, to make sure coverage is adequate, and the requirement itself makes an applicability assessment of every requirement mandatory. Option A assumes a deeper framework covers everything: the Application Guidance says a stricter one should guide the scope, but only once the link is documented and coverage is checked.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a stricter framework should guide the scope, but only once each requirement is mapped to the planned tests and the coverage is judged sufficient.
wrong_explanations.B: A framework-based program is allowed and often helpful. The task is to reconcile it with the requirement, not to discard it.
wrong_explanations.C: Adding every step without mapping duplicates tests the framework already covers; due professional care weighs cost against benefit, and mapping first shows what is missing.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a framework-based program is allowed once mapped, and C, because adding every step before mapping duplicates work the framework may already cover.
Final two: D beats A because a framework adopted is not coverage shown; each requirement is mapped, and the mapping documented, before the program is relied on.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about IT control frameworks, treat the framework as a tool for coverage and the Topical Requirement as the minimum it must meet.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Planning around key risks and controls. Readiness to recover from a cyber incident
questions.question: Planning cybersecurity assurance at a Jordanian eye hospital, internal auditor Rami learns its incident response plan was approved last year and nightly backups always complete. Which matter must Rami MOST clearly assess?

options.A: Whether response and recovery are rehearsed at set intervals
options.B: Whether nightly backups finish within their scheduled window
options.C: Whether the board approved the incident response plan before its use
options.D: Whether the response plan follows the latest NIST framework template

questions.key_concept: The Cybersecurity Topical Requirement asks whether incident response and recovery are tested periodically; written plans and completed backups do not show recovery works.
questions.pre_read: A plan on paper and a backup that completes are claims. Ask what the requirement says shows the process works.
questions.correct_explanation: The Cybersecurity Topical Requirement's risk management section requires internal auditors to assess whether an incident response and recovery process exists, covering the stages from spotting an incident to learning from it, and whether it is tested periodically. An approved plan and completed backups do not show the hospital can recover. Option B checks a single routine: useful detail, but it says nothing about restoring service.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: backup completion is a useful control check, but a backup that is never restored proves little; the requirement asks whether the recovery process is tested.
wrong_explanations.C: The requirement does not ask for board approval of the response plan; it asks whether the process exists, covers its stages and is tested.
wrong_explanations.D: The requirement sets the baseline and names no framework; it asks whether a response and recovery process exists, covers its stages and is tested.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the requirement asks for a tested process, not board approval of the plan, and D, because it names no framework the plan must follow.
Final two: A beats B because a completed backup is not a tested recovery; the requirement asks whether response and recovery are tested periodically.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about readiness, prefer evidence that recovery was tried and timed over evidence that plans and backups exist.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Choosing the engagement approach. Changing tests between agile cycles
questions.question: In an agile engagement on a Chilean retailer's checkout app, internal auditor Matías adds tests to the next cycle; supervisor Paula holds delegated approval. What do the Standards MOST clearly require for those tests?

options.A: A record of the added tests in the cycle's backlog
options.B: Paula's approval of the cycle's changes at its closing review
options.C: The board's approval of the change in approach
options.D: Paula's approval of the revised program as the change is made

questions.key_concept: Agile work keeps the work program rules: each revision is approved by the chief audit executive or a delegate promptly, as it is made.
questions.pre_read: An agile approach changes how often the program changes, not who approves it or when.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.6 requires the chief audit executive to approve the work program before it is carried out and promptly whenever it changes, and Standard 12.3 lets a qualified engagement supervisor such as Paula approve those changes. An agile approach changes the program every cycle, so each revision is approved as it is made. Option B keeps the approval but moves it to the cycle's closing review, after the tests it should govern.

wrong_explanations.A: Recording the change is good practice, but a record is not an approval; Standard 13.6 requires the revised work program to be approved promptly.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the approval is right but late. Standard 13.6 asks for approval promptly when the program changes, not at a review after the cycle's tests have run.
wrong_explanations.C: The board approves the internal audit plan, not an engagement's approach or work program. Approval of the program sits with the chief audit executive or a delegate.

tips: Eliminate: A, because recording a change does not approve it, and C, because the board does not approve an engagement's work program.
Final two: D beats B because a revised work program is approved promptly as it changes, not at a review after its tests have run.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about agile, remote or integrated work, the approach changes; the requirements for approvals and evidence do not.

questions.subtopic: 2A5 Detailed engagement risk assessment. Cyber risk in a business process engagement
questions.question: Planning assurance on a Moroccan insurer's claims payments, internal auditor Yassine finds claims arrive through a public web portal; the plan gives the engagement no cybersecurity scope. Which approach to cyber risk is BEST?

options.A: Leave cyber risk out, as the plan gives it no scope here
options.B: Assess the portal's cyber risks in this engagement's risk assessment
options.C: Refer the portal's cyber risks to IT for its own review
options.D: Propose a separate cybersecurity engagement on the portal next year

questions.key_concept: IT and cyber risks are pervasive: an engagement on a business process assesses the cyber risks in that process, whatever the plan's label.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the plan's subject limits which risks to that subject are assessed.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 requires Yassine to identify the potentially significant risks to the claims activity's objectives, and the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement's user guide expects cyber risks to be assessed when planning assurance engagements on business processes. Once identified, the requirement is assessed for applicability, and any exclusion is documented. Option D may follow later, but it leaves this year's claims assurance blind to a risk inside the process.

wrong_explanations.A: The plan names the engagement's subject, not a limit on which risks to it are assessed. Standard 13.2 asks for the significant risks to the activity, cyber risks included.
wrong_explanations.C: IT's own review is management's work and may help, but it does not replace the engagement's risk assessment of risks in the process under review.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a separate engagement may be worth proposing, but this engagement still assesses the cyber risks in the claims process it covers now.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the plan's subject does not limit which risks are assessed, and C, because IT's own review cannot stand in for the engagement's risk assessment.
Final two: B beats D because cyber risk inside the claims process is assessed in this engagement now; a future engagement does not cover this year's work.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, treat IT and cyber risks as pervasive: weigh them in any process engagement whose activity runs on systems.

questions.subtopic: 2A5 Detailed engagement risk assessment. A rating scale with no amounts
questions.question: Two internal auditors score one pharmacy risk 2 and 4 on their Brazilian hospital engagement's own impact bands, labeled only minor to severe; the board states its tolerable stock loss. Which fix is BEST?

options.A: Give each impact level an amount linked to the loss tolerance
options.B: Average the two impact scores, then compare the result with the tolerance
options.C: Use the higher score, so the stock loss risk is not understated
options.D: Have the engagement supervisor settle the score for this risk

questions.key_concept: Ratings are comparable only on a defined scale; tie impact bands to the organization's risk tolerance and thresholds where they exist.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the two scores differ, and whether the fix should cover this risk or every risk on the scale.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 requires the organization's risk tolerance to be gathered where it is set and each risk's significance to be evaluated, and its considerations estimate significance from impact and likelihood. Bands defined in amounts tied to the hospital's stated tolerance let both auditors, and the next risk, land on the same rating. Option D settles this one score, but the next risk would split the auditors again, because the scale itself defines nothing.

wrong_explanations.B: An average compared with the tolerance still rests on bands with no defined amounts, so a 3 means no more than a 2 or a 4.
wrong_explanations.C: Taking the higher score builds in a bias without defining the scale; the next pair of ratings can split again, and overrated risks pull hours from others.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a supervisor can resolve a single difference of judgment, but the cause is an undefined scale, which will split the next rating too.

tips: Eliminate: B, because averaging scores on an undefined scale leaves its flaw in place, and C, because taking the higher score adds bias without fixing the scale.
Final two: A beats D because the cause is a scale with no defined amounts; tying it to the organization's tolerance fixes every rating, not one.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about rating risks, prefer the organization's own yardsticks, such as risk tolerance and thresholds, over scores settled case by case.

questions.subtopic: 2A6 Procedures and the work program. A gap that blocks approval
questions.question: Engagement supervisor Chen, who holds the chief audit executive's delegated approval, reviews the draft work program for a Taiwanese chipmaker's scrap sales engagement. Which gap MOST clearly prevents Chen from approving it?

options.A: A sampled test omits whether its results can be projected
options.B: The revenue objective has tasks but no criteria named
options.C: The program has no column for reviewers' sign-off dates
options.D: The tasks show no budgeted hours against each step

questions.key_concept: A work program must name, for each objective, its criteria, tasks, methods and tools, and the internal auditor assigned; other details are good practice.
questions.pre_read: Sort the gaps into what Standard 13.6 requires and what its considerations recommend.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.6 requires the work program to name, for each objective, the criteria used to evaluate it, the tasks, the methods and tools, and the internal auditor assigned, and to be approved before it is carried out. A missing criterion breaks a requirement, so the program cannot yet be approved. Option A breaks a consideration: recording whether sample results can be projected is good practice, a should.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the considerations say a sampling plan should record whether results can be projected, but that is a should; a missing criterion breaks a requirement.
wrong_explanations.C: A place for sign-offs is a consideration of Standard 13.6, good practice for showing who did and reviewed each task, but not a requirement.
wrong_explanations.D: Budgeted hours help the supervisor assign staff under Standard 13.5's considerations, but the work program requirement does not list them.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a sign-off column is good practice, not a requirement, and D, because hours budgets help staffing but are not a required element of the program.
Final two: B beats A because criteria for each objective are a must of Standard 13.6, while projecting sample results is a should.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about a work program, check the four musts: criteria for each objective, tasks, methods and tools, and who does each task.

questions.subtopic: 2A6 Procedures and the work program. A procedure that judges design
questions.question: Before testing whether a Polish bus operator's monthly fuel-card review is done, internal auditor Tomasz wants to judge whether the review could catch misuse at all. Which procedure BEST does that?

options.A: Reperform the review for months drawn across the year
options.B: Time each review, comparing its cost with the misuse losses it prevents
options.C: Survey card holders on whether misuse would be noticed
options.D: Walk through one review, noting what the reviewer's report shows

questions.key_concept: Design asks whether a control, performed as intended, could catch the risk; a walk-through shows what the performer actually sees.
questions.pre_read: Separate three questions: could the control catch misuse, was it done, and is it worth its cost?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 requires Tomasz to understand how a process is intended to operate, and its considerations judge whether control design is adequate apart from whether the control operates. Walking through one review, a form of direct observation in Standard 14.1's considerations, shows what the reviewer's report can reveal, such as each card's fuel against its vehicle. Option A answers the operating question, whether the review is done, not whether it could catch misuse.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: reperformance across the year is a strong test of operation, but a faithfully done review that cannot see misuse still fails; it does not answer the design question.
wrong_explanations.B: Comparing cost with losses is an efficiency question: whether the review is worth what it costs, not whether it could catch misuse.
wrong_explanations.C: Card holders' views are opinions from people the review restrains. A survey gathers perceptions; it does not show what the review can detect.

tips: Eliminate: B, because comparing cost with losses tests efficiency, not design, and C, because card holders' opinions do not show what the review can detect.
Final two: D beats A because design asks whether the review could catch misuse; reperformance shows it was done, not that it can see the problem.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about control design, look for a procedure that shows what the control can see or stop, not how often it was performed.

questions.subtopic: 2A6 Procedures and the work program. A population that changed midyear
questions.question: Internal auditor Fatoumata plans to test 30 system approvals for an objective covering a Malian telecom's full year of refunds; approvals moved from paper to the billing system in July. Which revision is BEST?

options.A: Also test paper approvals from January to June, as a separate population
options.B: Spread the 30 system approvals evenly from July to December
options.C: Test the system's approval setting once, as the control is automated
options.D: Narrow the objective to July onward, noting paper months as untested

questions.key_concept: Evidence must cover the period the objective names; a control that changed midyear gives two populations, and each needs testing.
questions.pre_read: Ask which months the objective covers and which months the planned sample can speak for.
questions.correct_explanation: The objective covers the whole year, so the evidence must too: under Standard 14.1 it must be sufficient for a competent person to reach the same conclusion, and Standard 13.6's considerations have a sampling plan record its population. Paper approvals before July are a different population under a different control, so they are tested separately. Option B improves the second half's spread but leaves January to June untested.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: spreading the sample across July to December is sound, but it still says nothing about the paper approvals that ran from January to June.
wrong_explanations.C: Testing an automated setting can suit the months the system ran, but it covers neither the paper approvals before July nor the full year the objective names.
wrong_explanations.D: Narrowing an objective needs the chief audit executive's or a delegate's approval, and nothing here calls for it; the paper months are another population to test.

tips: Eliminate: C, because one test of an automated setting cannot cover the paper months, and D, because narrowing the objective needs approval and nothing here calls for it.
Final two: A beats B because a control that changed midyear gives two populations; spreading the sample within one half leaves the other untested.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about samples, match the population to the period the objective covers, and test each version of a control that changed.

questions.subtopic: 2A7 Resources and skills for the engagement. A data tool new to the function
questions.question: Internal auditor Bat-Erdene plans to analyze a Mongolian airline's two million booking records with a data tool new to the function. What MOST needs to be in place before the engagement relies on it?

options.A: The revenue manager's approval to use the tool on the airline's data
options.B: A vendor's written statement that the tool's outputs are accurate and complete
options.C: Training in the tool, and set-up agreed with IT and information security
options.D: The board's approval of the tool before its first engagement use

questions.key_concept: New audit technology needs trained users and a set-up agreed with IT and information security before results are relied on.
questions.pre_read: Ask what Standard 10.3 says must come with new technology, and who approves technology funding rather than its use.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 10.3 requires the chief audit executive, when bringing in new technology, to train internal auditors in using it and to work with the organization's IT and information security functions so it is set up properly. A tool nobody is trained on, set up outside those functions, risks wrong results and exposed data. Option D stretches a consideration: technology funding requests go to the board and senior management, not each tool's use.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit's access to records rests on its mandate, which the charter records, so the revenue manager arranges access rather than approving which audit tools are used.
wrong_explanations.B: A vendor's claim about its own product does not show the tool works on this data, and it replaces neither training nor a proper set-up.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: funding requests for technology go to the board and senior management, but the Standards do not make the board approve each tool before an engagement uses it.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the data owner arranges access but does not approve internal audit's tools, and B, because a vendor's claim replaces neither training nor a proper set-up.
Final two: C beats D because Standard 10.3 requires training and set-up with IT and information security; board approval covers technology funding, not each tool's use.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about new audit technology, look for trained users and a set-up agreed with IT and security before any reliance on results.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Engagement objectives and scope. Files withheld at planning
questions.question: Planning assurance on a Dutch insurer's claims paid this year, engagement supervisor Femke learns the claims director will withhold 40 claim files, calling them sensitive. What should Femke do FIRST?

options.A: Record the 40 files as excluded, giving the director's reason
options.B: Record a scope limitation and discuss it with claims management
options.C: Record a scope limitation for the chief audit executive to elevate
options.D: Test the other claims, explaining the 40 in the final communication

questions.key_concept: Withheld records found at planning are a scope limitation: record it and discuss it with management; the chief audit executive elevates only if unresolved.
questions.pre_read: Ask what stage the restriction is at: just found, or already discussed with management without success.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.3 counts blocked access to data and information as a scope limitation in assurance work and has it raised with management as soon as it comes to light, aiming to settle it; the workpapers record it. Femke has only just learned of it, so the talk with claims management comes first. Option C skips that step: the chief audit executive takes a limitation to the board only when management does not resolve it.

wrong_explanations.A: A recorded exclusion fits advisory work or a Topical Requirement's risk-based exclusions; in assurance, withheld files are a scope limitation whatever reason is given.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: elevation is right once talks with management have failed. Here the restriction has only just come to light, so management hears it first.
wrong_explanations.D: Explaining it in the final communication comes later, after discussion and any elevation; testing around it now leaves the restriction unchallenged.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a recorded exclusion fits advisory or Topical Requirement scoping, not withheld assurance files, and D, because the final communication explains a limitation only after it is discussed.
Final two: B beats C because a scope limitation is discussed with management when it comes to light; the chief audit executive elevates it to the board only if that fails.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about blocked access, find the stage first: just found means discuss with management; discussed and unresolved means the chief audit executive elevates.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Engagement objectives and scope. A request to add work in the same days
questions.question: During planning, a Peruvian mine's finance director asks internal auditor Rosa to add fuel-tax refunds to the 20-day fuel purchases assurance engagement, same end date; supervisor Hugo holds delegated approval. Which response is BEST?

options.A: Agree the added work with the finance director, who asked for it
options.B: Decline the refunds, proposing them for a later engagement instead
options.C: Raise it with Hugo as a scope change fitted into 20 days
options.D: Raise it with Hugo as a scope limitation on the existing work

questions.key_concept: A request to add work without more time can squeeze planned work, so weigh it as a possible scope limitation, not just a change.
questions.pre_read: Check what stays fixed when work is added: the days and the end date decide whether the request threatens the original objectives.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.3's considerations say a stakeholder's wish to add or drop items, or to cap how long the work takes, may itself be a scope limitation. Here both apply: more work, same days. Rosa takes it to Hugo, who approves any change, as a limitation on the work already planned. Option C treats it as an ordinary change and squeezes both into 20 days, leaving the original objectives at risk.

wrong_explanations.A: In advisory work the scope is usually agreed with the requesting management; in assurance, internal auditors set it and the chief audit executive or a delegate approves changes.
wrong_explanations.B: Declining could be right if the refunds carry little risk, but the choice is not Rosa's alone, and the request has not yet been weighed against the objectives.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: an added area is a scope change needing approval, but fitting it into the same 20 days ignores that the original work may no longer get done.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the requester agrees scope only in advisory work, and B, because Rosa cannot settle the request alone before weighing it.
Final two: D beats C because the end date is fixed, so the request may stop the planned work; approving it as a change does not address that.
Exam cue: on CIA questions where a stakeholder adds, drops or shortens work, ask whether what remains still reaches every objective; if not, think scope limitation.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Planning around key risks and controls. A new tool beside an unchanged risk register
questions.question: Planning cybersecurity assurance at a Greek shipping firm, internal auditor Nikos learns staff now draft client emails with an AI chatbot; the risk register has not changed in two years. Which matter MOST needs assessing?

options.A: Whether the chatbot's drafts to clients are accurate and courteous
options.B: Whether each listed cyber risk has an owner and fix date
options.C: Whether a process spots and reports threats from new technology
options.D: Whether staff passed this year's simulated phishing tests

questions.key_concept: The Cybersecurity Topical Requirement asks whether management watches for emerging threats; a new tool beside a stale risk register points there first.
questions.pre_read: Link each fact in the stem to an area the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement covers, then ask which area the facts most call into question.
questions.correct_explanation: The Cybersecurity Topical Requirement has internal auditors assess whether management keeps watch for new threats and weaknesses and reports them, and its user guide names new technology such as artificial intelligence. A tool taken up while the register stayed unchanged for two years suggests that watch is not working. Option B checks owners and dates for risks already listed, which says nothing about threats the register never captured.

wrong_explanations.A: Accuracy and courtesy of replies are quality matters for a customer service or AI governance review, not the cyber risks this engagement assesses.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: owners and fix dates for listed risks are part of cyber risk management, but a stale register's gap is the threats it never captured.
wrong_explanations.D: Phishing tests are one way the user guide suggests checking awareness, but nothing in the stem points to awareness as the weakness.

tips: Eliminate: A, because reply quality is not a cybersecurity matter, and D, because nothing in the facts points to staff awareness.
Final two: C beats B because a new tool and an unchanged register suggest emerging threats go unwatched; owners for listed risks cannot fix what was never listed.
Exam cue: on CIA cyber planning questions, a new technology plus an old risk register points to the process for spotting emerging threats.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Choosing the engagement approach. A project plan with no task owners
questions.question: Supervisor Kadri's draft work program for an Estonian agency's e-signature engagement gives each objective's criteria, tasks, methods and tools, with hours and dates per task. What MOST clearly must be added before approval?

options.A: The internal auditor who will carry out each step
options.B: A milestone marking the close of each fieldwork phase
options.C: A weekly progress call agreed with the agency's managers
options.D: A column comparing hours used with hours budgeted

questions.key_concept: Milestones, update calls and hours tracking are good project practice; naming who performs each task is what the work program must contain.
questions.pre_read: Sort the project features into what Standard 13.6 requires in a work program and what other considerations only recommend.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.6 requires the work program to set out the criteria for each objective, the tasks, the methods and tools, and the internal auditors assigned to each task, and the chief audit executive or a delegate approves it before work starts. Kadri's draft has everything but the owners. Option C reflects Standard 13.1's considerations on agreeing how often management is updated, which is good practice, not a work program requirement.

wrong_explanations.B: Milestones are a useful project tool for tracking progress, but no Standard requires them in the work program.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Standard 13.1's considerations favor agreeing how often management is updated, a should; the owner of each task is a must of Standard 13.6.
wrong_explanations.D: Comparing actual with budgeted hours is something Standard 13.5's considerations say internal auditors may do to improve later planning; it is optional.

tips: Eliminate: B, because milestones are project practice no Standard requires, and D, because hours tracking is an optional aid to later planning.
Final two: A beats C because a named owner for each task is required in the work program, while agreed update calls are a should.
Exam cue: on CIA questions that treat an engagement as a project, separate the work program's four musts from scheduling and reporting habits.

questions.subtopic: 2A5 Detailed engagement risk assessment. Topical Requirement applicability judged on inherent risk
questions.question: Awa, an internal auditor on a Senegalese utility's payroll assurance engagement, finds the payroll system reachable from the internet; IT reports strong, untested controls. Which applicability test for the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement is BEST?

options.A: The risk net of IT's reported controls, against the critical threshold
options.B: Whether cybersecurity is the subject the plan gave this engagement
options.C: The risk before IT's reported controls, against the critical threshold
options.D: Whether management has asked internal audit for cyber assurance

questions.key_concept: When a Topical Requirement's topic surfaces in another engagement, applicability turns on inherent risk, before untested controls, compared with the critical threshold.
questions.pre_read: Name the trigger in play: a planned topic, a request, or a topic found during another engagement. Then ask which risk rating that trigger uses.
questions.correct_explanation: A Topical Requirement applies when its topic is identified during an engagement, and the Topical Requirements Application Guidance says to judge that on inherent risk: impact and likelihood before controls, set against the critical threshold tied to risk appetite. IT's controls are untested, so counting them first, as option A does, could rule the requirement out on an unproven claim. If the inherent risk passes the threshold, Awa applies the requirements that fit it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the critical threshold is the right yardstick, but for inherent risk. Rating after controls nobody has tested could rule the requirement out on IT's word alone.
wrong_explanations.B: The plan's subject is one trigger. A topic identified during another engagement, as here, is a separate trigger, so payroll being the subject settles nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: A request outside the plan is a third trigger. No request is needed when the topic surfaces during an engagement.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a planned subject is only one trigger, and D, because a request is another; neither covers a topic found during this payroll engagement.
Final two: C beats A because applicability rests on inherent risk; untested controls cannot lower the rating that decides whether the requirement applies.
Exam cue: on CIA questions where a Topical Requirement's topic turns up mid-engagement, rate the inherent risk against the critical threshold before counting any controls.

questions.subtopic: 2A6 Procedures and the work program. A design gap found before operating tests
questions.question: Walking through a Botswanan bank's monthly suspense-account reconciliation, internal auditor Kago finds it leaves out manual journals, most of the account's entries; the program next tests 25 reconciliations. Which step is BEST?

options.A: Test the 25 reconciliations, as the approved program sets out
options.B: Note a potential finding, and seek approval to size its effect instead
options.C: Ask the finance manager to add manual journals before testing goes on
options.D: Judge the design from reviewer sign-offs found on the 25 reconciliations

questions.key_concept: When a walk-through shows a control cannot cover the risk, note the design gap and redirect testing to its effect; proving faithful performance adds little.
questions.pre_read: Ask two questions: could the reconciliation catch the problem if done perfectly, and what would 25 tests of it then prove?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.2, a gap between what should be and what is becomes a potential finding Kago must record and probe further, and extra analysis means an adjusted work program approved by the chief audit executive or delegate. Standard 13.2's considerations use design results to pick the controls worth testing for operation. A reconciliation that misses most entries fails on design, so option A's 25 tests would show only that a flawed control was done.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the approved program is the starting point, but it changes when the work shows the need; testing faithful performance of a control that misses most entries proves little.
wrong_explanations.C: Deciding and directing the fix is management's role; Kago reports the gap and its effect, and management then owns the action.
wrong_explanations.D: Sign-offs show the reconciliation was done, an operating question. They cannot show it covers manual journals, which is the design question.

tips: Eliminate: C, because fixing the control is management's job, and D, because sign-offs show performance, not whether the design can catch the risk.
Final two: B beats A because a design gap is noted and its effect sized; operating tests on a control that cannot work add little value.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a design failure found in a walk-through usually changes the planned tests, with approval, rather than being tested for operation.

questions.subtopic: 2A6 Procedures and the work program. A sample that cannot find the exception
questions.question: Reviewing a Czech brewer's payments work program, engagement supervisor Hana sees one objective ask whether any payment went out unapproved; its task samples 40 payments from the approvals log. Which weakness MOST undermines the program?

options.A: Its population holds only payments that someone signed off
options.B: The 40 payments have no stated basis for the sample size
options.C: The task has no place for a reviewer's initials and date
options.D: The design evaluation sits in a separate workpaper

questions.key_concept: A work program is adequate only if its tasks can achieve each objective; a sample drawn from approved items can never reveal an unapproved one.
questions.pre_read: Before weighing documentation gaps, ask whether each task could ever produce the evidence its objective needs.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.6 requires a work program whose tasks achieve the engagement objectives. Every payment in the approvals log was, by definition, approved, so no sample from it can show whether a payment went out without approval; the task needs all payments made, such as the bank's payment records. Option B is a real gap in Standard 13.6's considerations, which ask for the sampling basis, but it is a should and leaves the test usable.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the considerations ask the program to record the sampling method, population and size, a should; even a well-sized sample from this log cannot find an unapproved payment.
wrong_explanations.C: A place for initials and dates is a should in Standard 13.6's considerations; its absence weakens the record, not the task's ability to meet the objective.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 13.6's considerations allow the design evaluation in the work program or a separate workpaper, so this is not a weakness.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a sign-off place is good practice only, and D, because a separate design workpaper is expressly allowed.
Final two: A beats B because a sample from approved items can never find an unapproved one; the sample-size basis is a should that leaves the test usable.
Exam cue: on CIA questions judging a work program, first ask whether each task could produce the evidence its objective needs, then look at documentation.

questions.subtopic: 2A6 Procedures and the work program. Testing that leavers lose system access
questions.question: In internal auditor Ruta's engagement on a Lithuanian bank's IT systems, one objective asks whether staff who leave lose their access to the loans system. Which test method BEST serves that objective?

options.A: Read the access policy's rules for removing leavers' rights
options.B: Get the system administrator's signed statement that leavers were removed
options.C: Match the current user list against HR's record of leavers
options.D: Inspect a sample of removal requests HR sent to IT

questions.key_concept: For an access objective, compare who can still log in with an independent record of who has left; statements and request forms show less.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the objective needs to see: the state of access today, or a step in the process meant to lead to it.
questions.correct_explanation: The objective is about the system's actual state, so the test must show who can log in now. Matching the user list, ideally extracted by the auditor, against HR's leaver records compares two sources, one independent of IT, which Standard 14.1 says makes evidence more reliable. Option D tests only whether HR asked IT to remove access; a request sent is not access removed.

wrong_explanations.A: The policy is the criterion, the yardstick for removal; reading it shows what should happen, not whether access was actually removed.
wrong_explanations.B: A signed statement still comes from the person responsible for removing access, so it is neither independent nor corroborated evidence of the condition.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: removal requests test whether HR notified IT, a useful step for a different objective, but they cannot show that access was actually taken away.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a policy states criteria rather than the condition, and B, because a statement from the administrator is not independent evidence.
Final two: C beats D because the user list shows who can log in today; a request to remove access shows only that someone asked.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about IT access, test the system's actual state against an independent record rather than the paperwork meant to produce it.

questions.subtopic: 2A7 Resources and skills for the engagement. A budget with no money for site work
questions.question: Planning an Argentine olive oil exporter's engagement, internal auditor Martina finds the budget holds no travel, though two of three objectives need inspection of oil stored at a distant port. Which step is BEST?

options.A: Ask the chief audit executive to approve dropping the two port objectives
options.B: Show the chief audit executive the travel cost, to obtain the funds
options.C: Rely on photos and stock records the port staff send
options.D: Ask the audit committee chair directly for the travel funds

questions.key_concept: Short of money objectives need, seek it through the chief audit executive first; a smaller scope is a later option if funds cannot be found.
questions.pre_read: Ask what Standard 13.5 has internal auditors do when resources fall short, and when cutting the scope becomes an option.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.5 has internal auditors work out the financial resources each objective needs and, when what is available falls short, raise the gap with the chief audit executive so the money can be found. Martina shows what the port work costs. Option A jumps ahead: the considerations treat a reduced scope as a possible outcome only once the chief audit executive cannot obtain the resources.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a narrower scope may follow if the chief audit executive cannot find the money, but asking to drop objectives first skips the step of seeking it.
wrong_explanations.C: Photos and records from port staff are neither obtained directly nor independent, and the objectives need inspection, so this weakens evidence below what the work requires.
wrong_explanations.D: The board hears about resource limits from the chief audit executive; an internal auditor going straight to the audit committee chair bypasses that route.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the objectives need first-hand inspection, and D, because resource concerns reach the board through the chief audit executive.
Final two: B beats A because Standard 13.5 has the auditor seek the missing resources first; a reduced scope is the fallback when they cannot be obtained.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about an engagement short of money, people or tools, go first to the chief audit executive to obtain them, not to cut.

questions.subtopic: 2A7 Resources and skills for the engagement. Staffing a rule no auditor has applied
questions.question: Supervisor Yuki knows an insurance accounting rule and staffs an engagement on a Japanese insurer's reporting team's use of it; auditor Ren, with related experience, can take a course before fieldwork. Which staffing is BEST?

options.A: An outside specialist, as the rule is new to the auditors
options.B: A reporting team member, working under Yuki's close review
options.C: The most senior auditor, whose long experience spans most rules
options.D: Ren, once trained, with Yuki reviewing the work closely

questions.key_concept: Assign auditors who have or can attain the competency, through training and close supervision; never staff from the activity under review.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the skill can be attained in time, and who could review the work, before reaching for outside help.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 3.1 lets internal auditors take on work they have, or can attain, the competencies for, and its considerations count courses and supervised tasks during an engagement as ways to attain them. Ren has related experience and a course before fieldwork, and Yuki knows the rule; Standard 12.3 lets supervision deepen to match. Option A, an outside specialist, fits when no one can attain the skill in time, which is not so here.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the considerations point to outside providers when the function lacks a competency, but here Ren can attain it in time with training and Yuki's review.
wrong_explanations.B: Someone from the reporting team would be assessing their own team's work, so their objectivity is impaired; a guest auditor must come from outside the activity under review.
wrong_explanations.C: Seniority is not competency; years of other work do not show the knowledge this rule needs, and Standard 3.1 asks for the competencies the work requires.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a reporting team member cannot assess their own team's work, and C, because seniority does not supply the rule's knowledge.
Final two: D beats A because Ren can attain the competency in time through the course and Yuki's close review; outsourcing fits when no one can.
Exam cue: on CIA staffing questions, have or attain the skill first: training plus supervision often closes the gap before an outside specialist is needed.

questions.subtopic: 2A7 Resources and skills for the engagement. Narrowing a Topical Requirement engagement for lack of skills
questions.question: Internal auditor Ndapewa's cybersecurity assurance engagement at a Namibian bank needs cloud skills for two applicable control requirements, which the chief audit executive cannot obtain in time. Which statement about narrowing scope is MOST accurate?

options.A: The two may be excluded, citing the skills gap as the reason
options.B: The chief audit executive may approve it, as for any scope change
options.C: It needs a recorded rationale, agreed or approved by the board
options.D: The work may turn advisory, where conformance is recommended instead

questions.key_concept: Lack of skills does not waive a Topical Requirement: narrowing such an engagement for resource reasons needs a documented rationale and the board's agreement.
questions.pre_read: Separate an exclusion justified by the risk from one forced by resources; the Application Guidance treats them differently.
questions.correct_explanation: The Topical Requirements Application Guidance says a gap in capacity or skills does not waive the duty to apply an applicable requirement. Under Standard 8.2 the chief audit executive tells the board of the limitation and how it will be handled, and the guidance allows a narrower scope only with a documented rationale that the board agrees or approves. Option B states the ordinary rule for scope changes, which is not enough here.

wrong_explanations.A: Exclusions rest on the identified risk's nature or cause, with a documented reason. A skills gap is a resource limit, which the guidance says does not waive the requirement.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: under Standard 13.3 the chief audit executive approves scope changes, but for a Topical Requirement narrowed by resource limits the guidance adds the board's agreement.
wrong_explanations.D: The guidance suggests advisory use where a high-risk area is still immature, not as a route around an assurance engagement that lacks skills.

tips: Eliminate: A, because exclusions follow the risk, not the team's skills, and D, because turning advisory is meant for immature areas, not resource gaps.
Final two: C beats B because narrowing an applicable Topical Requirement for lack of resources needs a documented rationale and the board's agreement, beyond the usual approval.
Exam cue: on CIA questions where resources fall short on a Topical Requirement, expect the board to hear of it and to agree any narrower scope.
